_note: Curated plain-English shipping glossary. Terms are matched against headlines in the browser and turned into clickable buttons. 'short' is the one-line definition shown first; 'why' explains why the term matters, which is the part that actually teaches.

terms.short: A ship's daily earnings after voyage costs.
terms.long: Freight revenue minus voyage costs (fuel, port fees, canal tolls), divided by the number of days the voyage took. It converts a $/tonne cargo rate into a $/day figure.
terms.why: This is the number that decides whether an owner makes money. A headline freight rate alone doesn't tell you, because on a voyage charter the owner pays for the fuel.

terms.short: The price to hire a ship for one single voyage, right now.
terms.long: Agreed voyage by voyage at whatever the market will bear today, rather than fixed in advance.
terms.why: Spot rates swing violently — they can triple in weeks. Owners with lots of spot exposure make spectacular profits in a strong market and lose money in a weak one.

terms.short: Renting out a ship by the day for months or years.
terms.long: The charterer pays a fixed daily hire rate and takes on the fuel and port costs; the owner provides and crews the ship.
terms.why: It trades upside for certainty. A company on long time charters has predictable earnings; one on spot has a lottery ticket. Knowing the mix tells you how risky a shipping share is.

terms.short: Hiring a ship to move one cargo from A to B for a price per tonne.
terms.long: The owner keeps control of the ship and pays the voyage costs, including fuel.
terms.why: Because the owner pays for fuel here, a rise in bunker prices eats directly into their earnings even if the freight rate hasn't changed.

terms.short: Fuel for ships, and the act of refuelling.
terms.long: Mostly VLSFO today, with MGO for stricter emission zones and older IFO380 for ships fitted with scrubbers.
terms.why: Fuel is the biggest single voyage cost. It's the main reason a freight rate and an owner's actual profit move differently.

terms.short: The standard marine fuel since 2020, max 0.5% sulphur.
terms.long: Introduced to meet the IMO 2020 sulphur cap. It is the benchmark bunker grade at most ports.
terms.why: Its price is the single most useful cost number in shipping. Watch the gap to high-sulphur fuel: a wide gap makes scrubbers pay off.

terms.short: A cleaner, pricier distillate marine fuel.
terms.long: Used in emission control areas and by smaller vessels. Chemically closer to diesel than to residual fuel oil.
terms.why: It always costs more than VLSFO, so voyages through strict emission zones cost more to run.

terms.short: Cheap, high-sulphur residual fuel oil.
terms.long: Only legal to burn if the ship has a scrubber fitted to clean its exhaust.
terms.why: The discount to VLSFO is what repays the cost of installing a scrubber. A narrow spread makes scrubbers a bad investment.

terms.short: Equipment that cleans sulphur from a ship's exhaust.
terms.long: Lets a ship legally burn cheap high-sulphur fuel instead of pricier compliant fuel.
terms.why: A scrubber-fitted ship earns more when the HSFO–VLSFO spread is wide. It's a bet on that spread staying wide enough to repay the installation.

terms.short: One tonne of cargo moved one mile — demand measured by distance, not just volume.
terms.long: Multiplies cargo volume by how far it travels.
terms.why: The concept that explains most freight rate surprises. If the same oil travels further — say Europe buying from the US Gulf instead of Russia — tonne-miles rise and rates rise, even with zero extra oil produced.

terms.short: Sailing empty to reach the next cargo.
terms.long: The ship carries seawater for stability instead of cargo.
terms.why: Ballast days earn nothing but still burn fuel, so they drag down TCE. Trade patterns with long ballast legs need higher headline rates to be worth doing.

terms.short: How much weight a ship can carry, in tonnes.
terms.long: Includes cargo plus fuel, stores, crew and water.
terms.why: The standard measure of ship size, and the basis for every vessel class name you'll meet — a Capesize is simply a bulker of roughly 180,000 dwt.

terms.short: The biggest standard crude oil tanker, about 2 million barrels.
terms.long: Roughly 300,000 dwt. Used on long-haul routes, typically Arabian Gulf to Asia.
terms.why: The workhorse of long-distance oil trade and the most closely watched tanker class. Too big for the Panama Canal and most ports, so it serves deepwater terminals.

terms.short: A crude tanker sized to transit the Suez Canal fully laden, about 1 million barrels.
terms.long: Roughly 150,000 dwt.
terms.why: The flexible middle of the crude fleet. West Africa to Europe is its classic trade, and it gains whenever shorter-haul crude routes grow.

terms.short: A mid-size crude tanker of roughly 110,000 dwt, about 600,000 barrels.
terms.long: Named after the Average Freight Rate Assessment scale. The LR2 is the same hull carrying clean products.
terms.why: Serves shorter regional routes like the North Sea and Mediterranean, so it reacts to regional supply shifts faster than VLCCs.

terms.short: A large product tanker, same size as an Aframax but carrying refined products.
terms.long: Around 110,000 dwt with coated tanks so it can carry clean cargoes.
terms.why: Can switch between crude and clean trades depending on which pays better, which links the two markets together.

terms.short: The standard refined-product tanker, roughly 50,000 dwt.
terms.long: Carries gasoline, diesel and jet fuel on regional and transatlantic routes.
terms.why: The most numerous product tanker class. Its rates track refinery margins and where refineries are being built or closed.

terms.short: Refined fuels like gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
terms.long: Carried in coated or stainless tanks to avoid contamination.
terms.why: Clean tanker demand depends on where fuel is refined versus consumed. New refineries far from demand centres mean longer voyages and stronger rates.

terms.short: A tanker carrying crude oil or heavy fuel oil.
terms.long: The cargo leaves residue, so switching such a ship to clean cargoes needs expensive tank cleaning.
terms.why: The clean/dirty split is the basic division of the tanker market, and the two can move in opposite directions.

terms.short: The benchmark VLCC route: Arabian Gulf to China.
terms.long: A Baltic Exchange assessed route for 270,000 tonnes of crude.
terms.why: The single most quoted tanker rate in the world. When people say 'VLCC earnings', they usually mean this.

terms.short: The largest common dry bulk carrier, about 180,000 dwt.
terms.long: Too big for the Suez and Panama canals, so historically it sailed around the Cape of Good Hope.
terms.why: Carries mainly iron ore and coal, so its rates are effectively a bet on Chinese steel production.

terms.short: A bulker sized to fit the Panama Canal, around 80,000 dwt.
terms.long: Kamsarmax is a slightly larger modern variant at about 82,000 dwt.
terms.why: Carries coal and grain. More exposed to agricultural seasons and harvest timing than Capesizes are.

terms.short: A mid-size bulker of roughly 58,000 dwt with its own cranes.
terms.long: Being geared, it can load and discharge at ports without shore cranes.
terms.why: The most flexible bulker class. It serves minor bulks and poorer ports, so its rates reflect broad global trade rather than one commodity.

terms.short: The smallest Baltic-assessed bulker, about 38,000 dwt.
terms.long: Geared, and able to enter small and shallow ports.
terms.why: Carries minor bulks like cement, steel and fertiliser. Often the steadiest dry bulk segment because it's less tied to iron ore.

terms.short: The headline index of dry bulk freight rates.
terms.long: A weighted average of Capesize, Panamax, Supramax and Handysize earnings, published daily by the Baltic Exchange.
terms.why: Widely treated as a barometer of world trade. Treat that carefully — it's driven as much by how many ships exist as by how much cargo there is.

terms.short: The Capesize component of the Baltic Dry Index.
terms.long: Tracks earnings across the main iron ore and coal routes.
terms.why: The most volatile sub-index, and the main reason the BDI jumps around.

terms.short: The benchmark index for crude oil tanker rates.
terms.long: Covers the main dirty tanker routes.
terms.why: The tanker equivalent of the BDI, and the standard reference for crude freight.

terms.short: The benchmark index for refined product tanker rates.
terms.long: Covers the main clean product routes.
terms.why: Moves with refinery output and fuel trade patterns, often independently of crude tanker rates.

terms.short: The London body that publishes the benchmark freight indices.
terms.long: Assesses rates daily from a panel of shipbrokers.
terms.why: Its numbers settle real freight derivative contracts, which is why the full data is a paid product.

terms.short: A financial contract betting on future freight rates.
terms.long: Cash-settled against a Baltic index rather than involving an actual ship.
terms.why: FFA prices show what the market expects next, so they often move before physical rates do.

terms.short: When oil for later delivery costs more than oil today.
terms.long: The opposite is backwardation, where prompt oil is dearer.
terms.why: Steep contango makes it profitable to buy oil, store it and sell it forward — sometimes in chartered tankers. That removes ships from the trading fleet and lifts rates.

terms.short: When oil for immediate delivery costs more than oil later.
terms.long: Signals a tight prompt market.
terms.why: Discourages storage, so stored oil gets released and floating storage unwinds — returning ships to the fleet and softening rates.

terms.short: Using tankers as floating warehouses for oil.
terms.long: Cargo sits aboard at anchor instead of discharging.
terms.why: It takes ships out of the trading fleet without scrapping them, which can tighten the market sharply. Watch it whenever oil is in contango.

terms.short: The global benchmark price for crude oil.
terms.long: Based on North Sea crude; most internationally traded oil prices off it.
terms.why: Sets the cost of the fuel ships burn and influences how much oil moves and where. Note that high oil prices are not automatically good for tankers — what matters is volume and distance.

terms.short: The US benchmark crude price.
terms.long: Priced at Cushing, Oklahoma.
terms.why: The Brent–WTI gap decides whether US crude exports are profitable. A wide gap means more long-haul cargoes out of the US Gulf, which is good for tankers.

terms.short: Europe's benchmark natural gas price.
terms.long: A virtual trading hub in the Netherlands, quoted in euros per megawatt-hour.
terms.why: The TTF–JKM gap decides whether LNG cargoes sail to Europe or Asia. That choice changes voyage distances and therefore LNG shipping demand.

terms.short: The benchmark LNG price for North East Asia.
terms.long: Assessed in dollars per million British thermal units.
terms.why: When JKM trades well above TTF, cargoes head to Asia on longer voyages, lifting tonne-mile demand for LNG carriers.

terms.short: The US benchmark natural gas price.
terms.long: A pipeline hub in Louisiana, priced in dollars per million British thermal units.
terms.why: Cheap Henry Hub gas relative to TTF and JKM is what makes US LNG exports profitable — and US exports are the long-haul cargoes that LNG shipping depends on.

terms.short: Natural gas chilled to liquid so it can be shipped.
terms.long: Cooled to about minus 162°C, shrinking it roughly 600 times.
terms.why: Liquefaction lets gas trade between continents instead of being stuck to pipelines, which created the whole LNG shipping market.

terms.short: Propane and butane, shipped as a liquid under pressure.
terms.long: A by-product of gas processing and oil refining.
terms.why: Mostly a US-to-Asia trade carried by VLGCs. Its rates follow US export volumes and the propane price gap between regions.

terms.short: The largest standard LPG carrier, around 84,000 cubic metres.
terms.long: The workhorse of long-haul LPG trade.
terms.why: Its earnings hinge on US Gulf to Asia volumes and on Panama Canal transit delays, which can add weeks to a voyage.

terms.short: The main raw material for steel, and the biggest dry bulk cargo.
terms.long: Shipped mostly from Australia and Brazil to China.
terms.why: Brazil is far further from China than Australia, so a shift in sourcing between them changes tonne-mile demand and Capesize rates without changing total volume.

terms.short: A ship on order at a shipyard but not yet delivered.
terms.long: The orderbook is the total on order, usually quoted as a percentage of the existing fleet.
terms.why: The best early warning in shipping. A large orderbook means a wave of supply in two to three years, which caps future rates however strong demand looks today.

terms.short: Selling an old ship to be broken up for steel.
terms.long: Mostly done in India, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Turkey.
terms.why: The only way the fleet shrinks. Heavy scrapping in a weak market is what eventually sets up the next upturn.

terms.short: How much of the fleet is actually employed.
terms.long: Effective supply after allowing for ships idle, in dock, storing cargo or sailing slowly.
terms.why: Freight rates are wildly non-linear in utilisation. Near full employment, a 1% change in supply can double or halve rates — which is why shipping is so volatile.

terms.short: Ships queueing to load or discharge.
terms.long: Waiting time at anchor outside a port.
terms.why: Congestion soaks up ships without any extra cargo moving, tightening effective supply. It acts just like a fleet reduction while it lasts.

terms.short: A penalty the charterer pays when loading or discharging runs late.
terms.long: Charged per day beyond the agreed laytime.
terms.why: In congested markets demurrage can become a serious part of an owner's income.

terms.short: The time allowed for loading and unloading cargo.
terms.long: Agreed in the charter contract.
terms.why: The line between normal operations and demurrage charges.

terms.short: Whoever hires the ship.
terms.long: Often an oil major, commodity trader, miner or retailer.
terms.why: Charterers sit on the other side of every freight negotiation. Who they are tells you a lot about a trade's reliability.

terms.short: Whoever owns the vessel and earns the freight.
terms.long: May operate the ship themselves or hand it to a manager or pool.
terms.why: Listed shipping companies are mostly owners, so their earnings are freight income minus ship costs.

terms.short: Several owners putting ships into one fleet and sharing the earnings.
terms.long: A pool manager markets the ships jointly and distributes revenue by an agreed formula.
terms.why: Gives small owners the scale and route coverage of a large fleet, and smooths out individual voyage luck.

terms.short: Linking voyages so a ship carries cargo on more legs.
terms.long: Planning routes that avoid sailing empty between cargoes.
terms.why: Cuts ballast days, which directly raises TCE. Good operators earn more than rivals on identical ships this way.

terms.short: The daily cost of running a ship, excluding fuel.
terms.long: Crew, insurance, stores, repairs and management.
terms.why: The breakeven floor. Comparing OPEX against TCE tells you whether an owner is making or losing money each day.

terms.short: The daily rate an owner must earn to cover all cash costs.
terms.long: OPEX plus debt service, drydocking and overheads.
terms.why: The single most useful figure for judging a shipping share. Below it the company burns cash; well above it, profits compound fast.

terms.short: What a shipping company's ships are worth, minus its debt.
terms.long: Based on broker valuations of each vessel.
terms.why: Shipping shares often trade at a discount or premium to NAV. It's the standard yardstick for whether a share looks cheap.

terms.short: Buying ships cheap in a downturn to sell dear in an upturn.
terms.long: Profiting from the change in vessel values rather than from freight income.
terms.why: Ship values swing even more than rates, so timing the cycle has historically made more money in shipping than operating well.

terms.short: Taking a ship out of the water for inspection and repair.
terms.long: Required by class rules, usually every two and a half to five years.
terms.why: Costs money and removes the ship from earning for weeks. A heavy drydocking schedule dents a quarter's results.

terms.short: A body that certifies a ship is built and maintained to standard.
terms.long: DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS are among the largest.
terms.why: No class certificate means no insurance and no cargo. Class rules effectively set the maintenance calendar.

terms.short: A mutual insurer covering an owner's third-party liabilities.
terms.long: Owned by its shipowner members.
terms.why: Loss of P&I cover effectively stops a ship trading, which is why insurance is central to how sanctions are enforced.

terms.short: Legal restrictions on trading with certain countries or cargoes.
terms.long: In shipping these commonly work through insurance and financing rather than direct bans.
terms.why: Sanctions rarely reduce how much oil moves; they reroute it. Longer reroutes raise tonne-miles, which is why sanctions have often *helped* tanker rates.

terms.short: Ageing tankers moving sanctioned oil outside mainstream insurance.
terms.long: Typically older ships with opaque ownership that disable tracking signals.
terms.why: It splits the tanker market in two. Removing these old ships from the mainstream fleet tightens compliant tonnage and supports rates for everyone else.

terms.short: A transponder broadcasting a ship's identity and position.
terms.long: Required for safety and the basis of public ship-tracking sites.
terms.why: Makes shipping unusually transparent — you can watch cargo flows in near real time. Ships going dark is itself a signal.

terms.short: The UN agency that regulates shipping.
terms.long: Sets global rules on safety, pollution and emissions.
terms.why: Its rule changes reshape economics overnight. IMO 2020 rewrote the fuel market; carbon rules are doing the same to speed and fleet renewal.

terms.short: The 2020 rule capping marine fuel sulphur at 0.5%.
terms.long: Ships had to switch to VLSFO, fit a scrubber, or use alternative fuels.
terms.why: The textbook example of regulation reshaping a market: it created the VLSFO benchmark and the scrubber investment case.

terms.short: An annual efficiency rating for each ship, A to E.
terms.long: Measures carbon emitted per tonne-mile; poor ratings require a corrective plan.
terms.why: Pushes owners to slow down, since slower steaming cuts emissions. Slower ships means less effective fleet capacity, which supports rates.

terms.short: A one-off design-efficiency standard for existing ships.
terms.long: Often met by capping engine power.
terms.why: Power limits lower top speed across much of the fleet, quietly reducing supply.

terms.short: Deliberately sailing slower to burn less fuel.
terms.long: Fuel use rises roughly with the cube of speed, so small speed cuts save a lot.
terms.why: The fleet's shock absorber. In weak markets owners slow down, which soaks up surplus capacity; in strong markets they speed up and add supply.

terms.short: A sea region with stricter fuel and emission rules.
terms.long: Includes the North Sea, Baltic and North American coasts.
terms.why: Ships must burn cleaner, costlier fuel inside them, so voyages through ECAs cost more.

terms.short: The EU system making shipping pay for its carbon emissions.
terms.long: Operators surrender allowances for voyages touching the EU.
terms.why: Turns carbon into a direct voyage cost, changing which routes and ships are economic.

terms.short: The Egyptian canal linking the Mediterranean and Red Sea.
terms.long: Saves thousands of miles between Asia and Europe.
terms.why: When ships avoid it — as during Red Sea attacks — voyages lengthen dramatically. Tonne-miles jump and rates rise even with unchanged cargo volumes.

terms.short: The canal linking the Atlantic and Pacific.
terms.long: Transit slots are limited and auctioned when capacity is short.
terms.why: Drought has cut transits in recent years, hitting LPG and container routes hardest and forcing long detours.

terms.short: The route around southern Africa, used when Suez is avoided.
terms.long: Adds roughly 10 to 14 days on an Asia–Europe voyage.
terms.why: The main alternative to Suez, and the clearest real-world example of rerouting creating freight demand out of thin air.

terms.short: The profit from turning crude oil into refined products.
terms.long: The price gap between products and the crude they came from.
terms.why: Fat margins make refineries run hard, producing more cargo for product tankers. It's the best leading indicator for clean tanker demand.

terms.short: Profiting from the same commodity costing different amounts in different places.
terms.long: Open when the price gap exceeds the cost of shipping it.
terms.why: Arbitrage is what actually puts cargo on ships. When an arb opens, freight demand follows within weeks.

terms.short: Dry cargoes other than iron ore, coal and grain.
terms.long: Cement, fertiliser, steel products, bauxite, salt and sugar.
terms.why: Spread across many commodities and ports, so minor bulk demand is steadier than the major bulks.

terms.short: A ship with its own cargo cranes.
terms.long: Gearless ships depend on shore equipment.
terms.why: Gear lets smaller bulkers serve underdeveloped ports, which is exactly why they trade differently from Capesizes.

terms.short: The harvest periods that drive seasonal grain shipments.
terms.long: North American exports peak late in the year; South American exports peak in spring.
terms.why: One of the few genuinely predictable patterns in shipping, and the main seasonal driver of Panamax rates.

terms.short: Using financial contracts to lock in a future price.
terms.long: Owners and charterers use FFAs for freight and swaps for fuel.
terms.why: Explains why a company's reported earnings can diverge from spot rates — they may have fixed much of it in advance.

terms.short: The percentage scale tanker voyages are priced on.
terms.long: Every tanker route has a published reference rate called Worldscale 100, or 'flat rate', recalculated each January. A fixture at WS150 means 150% of that reference; WS50 means half of it.
terms.why: It lets one number compare routes of completely different lengths. But a Worldscale figure on its own tells you nothing about profit — you must convert it to TCE, daily earnings after fuel and port costs, before you know whether an owner is making money.

terms.short: The reference price that Worldscale 100 represents on a given route.
terms.long: Published annually by the Worldscale Association, based on a standard vessel, standard speed and the previous year's fuel prices and port costs.
terms.why: Because it resets every January, the same WS number can mean different money in different years. Comparing WS across years without checking the flat rate is a classic beginner's mistake.

terms.short: Daily earnings over a full there-and-back voyage, including the empty return.
terms.long: Calculated over the laden leg plus the ballast leg home, so the unpaid return journey is counted against the earnings.
terms.why: This is the honest version of a rate. A route can look excellent on the laden leg and still be poor business once you include sailing back empty to reposition for the next cargo.

terms.short: An average of several routes, used as one headline earnings figure per vessel size.
terms.long: The Capesize 5TC averages five routes, the Panamax 4TC four, the Supramax 10TC ten and the Handysize 7TC seven. Each is expressed as dollars per day.
terms.why: A single route can swing on one cargo. The basket smooths that out, which is why owners quote '5TC' when they describe what their Capesizes are earning.

terms.short: The Middle East Gulf — the world's largest crude loading region.
terms.long: Terminals including Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia, Kharg Island in Iran and Basrah in Iraq. Written AG or MEG depending on the broker.
terms.why: Most long-haul crude voyages start here, so anything affecting Gulf loadings or the Strait of Hormuz transit moves tanker rates worldwide.

terms.short: The narrow sea passage every Gulf cargo must transit.
terms.long: Between Oman and Iran, it is the only sea route out of the Middle East Gulf. Roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through it.
terms.why: There is no alternative route for most Gulf crude. Any threat to the strait affects insurance, routing and rates immediately, which is why brokers watch it constantly.

terms.short: Northwest Europe's refining and trading hub.
terms.long: ARA means Amsterdam, Rotterdam and Antwerp; UKC stretches from Le Havre up to Hamburg.
terms.why: Europe's main discharge region for crude and the main loading region for product exports, so a very large share of Atlantic tanker routes begins or ends here.

terms.short: The largest bulker that can enter the port of Newcastle, Australia — about 210,000 dwt.
terms.long: Slightly larger than a standard Capesize and used on the same iron ore and coal trades.
terms.why: Modern Newcastlemaxes burn less fuel per tonne carried than older Capesizes, so they out-earn them on the same route.

terms.short: Sailing with cargo aboard — the paid part of a voyage.
terms.long: The opposite of ballast, when the ship sails empty.
terms.why: Only laden days earn freight, but the owner pays for fuel and crew on every day. The ratio of laden to ballast days is what separates a good voyage from a bad one.

terms.short: The specific assumption a quoted rate is calculated on.
terms.long: When a report says a TCE is quoted 'basis Hound Point to Wilhelmshaven', those are the exact ports assumed.
terms.why: Two quotes for the same vessel class can differ simply because they assume different ports or speeds. Always check the basis before comparing.

terms.short: The Panamax component of the Baltic Dry Index.
terms.long: Tracks earnings for bulkers of roughly 82,000 dwt across four benchmark routes.
terms.why: Panamaxes carry coal and grain rather than iron ore, so this sub-index follows harvests and power demand while the Capesize index follows Chinese steel. When the two diverge, that tells you which part of the economy is moving.

terms.short: The Supramax component of the Baltic Dry Index.
terms.long: Tracks earnings for geared bulkers of roughly 58,000 dwt across ten routes.
terms.why: Supramaxes carry minor bulks to many ports rather than one commodity to a few, so this is the steadiest sub-index and the best read on broad global trade.
